claims.text: Applying a thin high-entropy-alloy coating to boride-based components will improve their resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
The initial boride-based components are as-fabricated and have no surface treatment or coating.
The proposed intervention is application of a thin, corrosion-resistant high-entropy-alloy surface coating.
Electrodeposition, sputtering, or laser cladding would be suitable techniques for applying the proposed coating.
The coated components are intended to operate in high-temperature molten aluminum.
The high-entropy-alloy coating acts as a physical barrier between molten aluminum and the boride-based substrate.
The coating prevents molten aluminum from contacting the underlying boride-based component.
The coating forms a dense layer.
The coating forms an adherent layer.
The coating is chemically stable under molten-aluminum exposure.
The coating prevents penetration of molten aluminum into the component.
Coated components will have a corrosion rate at least 50% lower than uncoated components.
Coating effectiveness depends on coating thickness.
Coating effectiveness depends on coating composition.
Coating effectiveness depends on coating microstructure.
Coating effectiveness depends on the operating conditions of the hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment.
The magnitude of corrosion improvement and the optimal coating composition and microstructure are uncertain.

contradictions.description: The prediction requires at least a 50% reduction in corrosion rate, but the falsification rule rejects the hypothesis only for no significant improvement. A statistically significant improvement below 50% would fail the stated prediction without necessarily satisfying the stated falsification rule.
